Q: Git commit error: cannot spawn gpg.exe: No such file or directory A:

Listening to the error, we can see the problem is that the CLI can't find gpg.exe:

Checking that folder, gpg.exe wasn't there (the folder was quite empty):

Thus I just tried to check if gpg.exe was in the same path, but under 32-bit Program Files folder (the one that doesn't end in x86). And in my case it was:

If this is your case, you just need to open your .gitconfig (in windows it is in your c:\users\your-user\).
Inside the file, just change the GPG -> program config to point to the right folder (in the case above, you only need to delete the " (x86)" in the end):

And there you go, signed commits working again!

If you can't find you gpg.exe file in any of those folders, try and make a global search for gpg.exe and, if there is no gpg.exe, reinstall GPG and adjust the folder in the .gitconfig file.

Q: How to give select query a name in Postgres A:
re-use → multiple times

per query

 in multiple queries

per session

 concurrent

sessions
with Common Table Expression T
prepared statement T
function/procedure T T T
view T T T
materialized view T T T
create table..as select T T T
cursor T

Within the same session and statement, you can re-use the CTE.
Within the same session, not in a single statement, you can prepare it: demo at db<>fiddle

prepare my_statement as
select distinct encoder.encoder enc, src_ip, encoder.datacenter 
from logical_service, unnest(tags) enc, encoder, mpeg_out 
where enc like 'encoder:%' 
  and substring(enc,9) = encoder.encoder 
  and logical_service.lid=mpeg_out.lid 
  and encoder.datacenter=mpeg_out.datacenter 
order by encoder.encoder

Then, execute it as many times as you need. To remove it, use deallocate:

execute my_statement;
deallocate my_statement;

Since prepared statements are tied to sessions, they don't interfere with each other, but it also means they aren't shareable. If you need your select statement to be re-usable by other users and concurrent sessions connected to this database, wrap it in a function:

create function my_select() returns table(
    enc encoder.encoder%type --input types taken directly from source
   ,src_ip logical_service.src_ip%type
   ,datacenter encoder.datacenter%type) stable--enough to make it inlineable here
begin atomic;--parsed at definition time, guards referential integrity
select distinct encoder.encoder enc, src_ip, encoder.datacenter 
from logical_service, unnest(tags) enc, encoder, mpeg_out 
where enc like 'encoder:%' 
  and substring(enc,9) = encoder.encoder 
  and logical_service.lid=mpeg_out.lid 
  and encoder.datacenter=mpeg_out.datacenter 
order by encoder.encoder;
end;

Then you can use it from other sessions on the db without each of them having to re-define it:

select * from my_select();
select (my_select()).*;

In both cases you need to be careful when combining this set-returning function with pulling data from tables or other SRFs. It's best to swap out your old-style comma joins for explicit ones both in the code that's re-using this select, and in the select itself:

select distinct encoder.encoder
     , src_ip
     , encoder.datacenter 
from logical_service
join lateral unnest(tags) as enc on enc like 'encoder:%' 
join encoder on substring(enc,9) = encoder.encoder 
join mpeg_out using(lid,datacenter)
order by encoder.encoder

Instead of using a function, you can also wrap it in a procedure, but those can only return a single row, which means you either need to make it return a cursor over the result set, or pack them in a composite or array, and let the caller handle unpacking it from the single returned row.

Another alternative is saving the select as a view:

create view my_view as select..

That's just as shareable and inlineable as a SQL function (Postgres rewriter simply substitutes the view body whenever you reference the view in a query) but you're limited to a single query (functions can run multiple) and it has to be a select or a values list (routines can do other things instead, or in addition to just returning data). Another variant is a materialized view:

create materialized view my_matview as select..

It caches the result set so the query doesn't have to be re-evaluated every time, and unlike regular views, you can create index on these. If the source data changes, you need to refresh materialized view my_matview;. A simpler version of that is a table directly based on your query

create table my_cached_select as select..

It just saves the result as a table but does not retain the definition, so it cannot be refreshed, only dropped and redefined.

If you mean to re-use the query within a session because you don't plan to use all its results at once, you can also declare a cursor and fetch rows gradually:

declare my_cursor cursor for select * from my_view;
fetch next from my_cursor;

It can't be shared by other users and sessions and it only lasts as long as your transaction. If you declare..with hold, it can be re-used by future transactions in your session, but that's because it caches a snapshot of the results on disk.

Q: What's the best way to unpivot data to create a structured database? A:

This is probably best handled by breaking the problem in 2 parts. Monthly payments and First/Last Payments. I've laid out one possible solution on your sheet in a tab called MK.Idea.

I used a SPLIT(FLATTEN( technique to generate both sets of cashflows and then a simple query to stack and order them.

This formula generated the monthly flows:

=ARRAYFORMULA(QUERY(SPLIT(FLATTEN('S1'!A2:A&"|"&'S1'!B2:B&"|"&MROUND(('S1'!D2:D-'S1'!E2:E-'S1'!I2:I)/'S1'!G2:G,100)&"|"&EDATE('S1'!H2:H,SEQUENCE(1,MAX('S1'!G2:G),0))&"|"&EDATE('S1'!H2:H,'S1'!G2:G)&"|"&"Monthly "&SEQUENCE(1,MAX('S1'!G2:G),1)),"|",0,0),"select Col4,Col1,Col2,Col6,Col3 where Col4<Col5"))

Q: Postgrespro : pg_probackup : error while executing add instance for pg_probackup A:

i found a solution, if you use pg_probackup std for vanilla postgres it won't work, you need to use pg_probackup for vanilla here is the repository where you need to download the desired version. before installation, you need to uninstall the previous version of pg_probackup.

http://repo.postgrespro.ru/pg_probackup/deb/pool/

after installing the vanilla version you will need to initialize the backup directory again and after that the instance will be successfully initialized

Q: Select rows with defined value + anything else A:

See examples with "window" functions

select *
from(
  select *
    ,sum(case when lang<>'SQL' then 1 else 0 end)over(partition by name) noSqlQty
    ,sum(case when lang='SQL' then 1 else 0 end)over(partition by name) SqlQty
  from employee
)t
where noSqlQty>0 and SqlQty>0;

Output

name lang noSqlQty SqlQty
Nick C# 1 1
Nick SQL 1 1

Or

select *
from(
  select *
    ,sum(case when lang='SQL' then 1 else 0 end)over(partition by name) isLangSql
    ,count(*)over(partition by name) langQty
  from employee
)t
where isLangSql>0 and langQty>1;
name lang isLangSql langQty
Nick C# 1 2
Nick SQL 1 2 
select *
from(
  select *
    ,lead(lang)over(partition by name order by case when lang='SQL'then 0 else 1 end) otherLang
  from employee
)t
where lang='SQL' and otherLang is not null;

As for your attempt to aggregate languages into a string and search for the necessary language codes in it (like substr(sum(lang),'SQL') != -1),
string and aggregate functions are DBMS-specific.
Specify the DBMS used.

Q: Difference between wait and sleep A:

Note that sleep and wait can be very powerful in conjunction, if you want your bash script to wait until it receives a signal. The following script will stop waiting for the sleep to finish if it receives one of the trapped signals.

With just the sleep alone, the signal wouldn't be encountered until the sleep has finished.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

trap 'echo SIGCONT received' SIGCONT  
trap 'echo SIGUSR1 received' SIGUSR1  
trap 'echo SIGINT received' SIGINT

sleep 100 &  
wait $!

Note that this is fragment is kept as simple as possible for demonstration purposes. You will probably want to kill the sleep that wait is waiting for when wait returns non-zero. (In fact, wait will return the signal number of the signal it was interrupted by.)
